lessons.lesson_title: What are the trade-offs between static and dynamic quantization?
lessons.content_html:
Definition

Static and dynamic quantization are two approaches to reduce model precision (e.g., FP32 → INT8) to improve efficiency.

  • Static quantization: Quantizes weights and activations before inference

  • Dynamic quantization: Quantizes weights ahead of time but activations during runtime

Why it is used

  • Improve inference speed

  • Reduce memory usage

  • Enable deployment on limited hardware

  • Balance performance vs accuracy

How it works (step-by-step)

Static quantization

  1. Use a calibration dataset

  2. Analyze activation ranges

  3. Quantize weights and activations offline

  4. Run inference fully in low precision

Dynamic quantization

  1. Quantize weights offline

  2. Keep activations in higher precision initially

  3. Quantize activations dynamically during inference

  4. Perform computation in mixed precision

Key components

  • Weights quantization: Common in both methods

  • Activation quantization: Static (precomputed) vs dynamic (runtime)

  • Calibration data: Required for static, not for dynamic

  • Inference engine support

Trade-offs

Performance

  • Static: Faster (fully quantized computation)

  • Dynamic: Slightly slower (runtime quantization overhead)

Accuracy

  • Static: Can be lower if calibration is poor

  • Dynamic: Often better accuracy (less aggressive quantization)

Complexity

  • Static: More complex (needs calibration dataset)

  • Dynamic: Easier to implement

Flexibility

  • Static: Less flexible (fixed quantization ranges)

  • Dynamic: More adaptable to varying inputs

Use cases

  • Static: Production systems needing maximum speed

  • Dynamic: Quick optimization with minimal setup

Advantages

Static quantization

  • Maximum speed improvement

  • Lower latency

  • Efficient for large-scale production

Dynamic quantization

  • Simple to apply

  • Better accuracy retention

  • No calibration data needed

Disadvantages

Static quantization

  • Requires calibration dataset

  • Sensitive to data distribution changes

Dynamic quantization

  • Slightly higher latency than static

  • Less performance gain

Real-world example

A chatbot model:

  • Static quantization used in production for fast responses

  • Dynamic quantization used during experimentation for easier setup

Short interview-ready answer

Static quantization precomputes quantization for both weights and activations, giving faster inference but requiring calibration and potentially impacting accuracy. Dynamic quantization only quantizes weights ahead of time and handles activations at runtime, making it easier to implement and often more accurate, but slightly slower.

lessons.lesson_title: What is pruning, and how does it reduce model size?
lessons.content_html:
Definition

Pruning is a model optimization technique where less important weights, neurons, or connections are removed from a neural network to make it smaller and more efficient.

Why it is used

  • Reduce model size

  • Speed up inference

  • Lower memory and compute usage

  • Enable deployment on resource-constrained devices

How it works (step-by-step)

  1. Start with a trained model

  2. Identify low-importance weights (e.g., near-zero values)

  3. Remove or zero out those weights

  4. Fine-tune the model to recover accuracy

  5. Deploy the smaller, optimized model

Key components

  • Importance criteria: Magnitude (small weights), gradients, or contribution

  • Pruning strategy: Which parts to remove (weights, neurons, layers)

  • Sparsity level: Percentage of parameters removed

  • Fine-tuning: Retraining after pruning to maintain performance

Common types

Unstructured pruning

  • Removes individual weights

  • High compression but irregular structure

Structured pruning

  • Removes entire neurons, filters, or layers

  • More hardware-friendly and faster

Magnitude-based pruning

  • Removes weights with smallest values

  • Most common approach

Iterative pruning

  • Gradually prune and retrain in cycles

  • Better accuracy retention

Advantages

  • Reduces model size significantly

  • Improves inference speed (especially structured pruning)

  • Lowers memory and compute requirements

  • Can be combined with quantization

Disadvantages

  • May reduce accuracy if over-pruned

  • Requires fine-tuning

  • Unstructured pruning may not give real speedup on all hardware

Real-world example

A large model is pruned by removing 30% of low-impact weights:

  • Model size decreases

  • Inference becomes faster

  • After fine-tuning, accuracy remains nearly the same

Short interview-ready answer

Pruning is a technique that removes less important weights or neurons from a trained model to reduce its size and improve efficiency. By eliminating low-impact parameters and fine-tuning the model, pruning achieves faster inference and lower memory usage with minimal loss in accuracy.

lessons.lesson_title: How does knowledge distillation create smaller, faster models?
lessons.content_html:
Definition

Knowledge distillation is a technique where a large, complex model (teacher) transfers its knowledge to a smaller model (student), making the student faster and more efficient while retaining similar performance.

Why it is used

  • Reduce model size and latency

  • Maintain performance close to large models

  • Enable deployment on limited hardware

  • Lower inference cost

How it works (step-by-step)

  1. Train or use a large, accurate teacher model

  2. Pass training data through the teacher to get outputs (soft probabilities/logits)

  3. Train the student model using:

    • Ground truth labels

    • Teacher’s soft outputs (knowledge)

  4. Student learns patterns and behavior of the teacher

  5. Deploy the smaller student model

Key components

  • Teacher model: Large, high-performance model

  • Student model: Smaller, efficient model

  • Soft labels: Teacher’s probability distribution (not just hard labels)

  • Temperature scaling: Smooths probabilities to transfer more knowledge

  • Loss function: Combines true labels + teacher guidance

Why it works

  • Soft labels contain richer information (class relationships)

  • Student learns not just the answer, but how the teacher thinks

  • Captures generalization ability of large models

Advantages

  • Smaller and faster models

  • Lower memory and compute cost

  • Retains much of teacher’s accuracy

  • Good for production deployment

Disadvantages

  • Requires a trained teacher model

  • Some accuracy loss is possible

  • Additional training step needed

Real-world example

A large LLM is too slow for production:

  • Use it as a teacher to train a smaller model

  • Student model runs faster with slightly lower but acceptable accuracy

  • Used in mobile or real-time applications

Short interview-ready answer

Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model using the outputs of a larger teacher model. By learning from the teacher’s soft predictions, the student captures important patterns and achieves similar performance while being faster and more efficient, making it suitable for production use.

lessons.lesson_title: What is LoRA, and why is it useful for efficient fine-tuning?
lessons.content_html:
Definition

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a fine-tuning technique where instead of updating all model weights, we add small trainable matrices (low-rank adapters) to certain layers and train only those.

Why it is used

  • Reduces training cost significantly

  • Requires much less memory (GPU-friendly)

  • Keeps base model unchanged

  • Enables fast and scalable fine-tuning

How it works (step-by-step)

  1. Start with a pre-trained model (weights are frozen)

  2. Inject small low-rank matrices (A and B) into layers (usually attention layers)

  3. Instead of updating original weights, train only these matrices

  4. During inference, combine base weights + LoRA updates

  5. Get task-specific behavior with minimal changes

Key components

  • Frozen base model: Original large model (unchanged)

  • Low-rank matrices (A, B): Small trainable parameters

  • Rank (r): Controls size of adapters (lower = more efficient)

  • Injection points: Typically attention layers

Why it works

  • Model updates often lie in a low-dimensional space

  • LoRA captures essential changes using small matrices

  • Avoids full fine-tuning of billions of parameters

Advantages

  • Very memory-efficient

  • Faster training

  • Easy to switch between multiple fine-tuned tasks

  • No need to store multiple full model copies

Disadvantages

  • Slightly lower performance than full fine-tuning (in some cases)

  • Requires choosing correct rank and layers

  • Not ideal for all types of tasks

Real-world example

A company fine-tunes a large LLM for customer support:

  • Instead of retraining entire model

  • Uses LoRA adapters for domain-specific knowledge

  • Saves cost and deploys quickly

Short interview-ready answer

LoRA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method where small low-rank matrices are added to a frozen pre-trained model, and only these are trained. This reduces memory and compute requirements while achieving near full fine-tuning performance, making it ideal for efficient and scalable LLM adaptation.

lessons.lesson_title: What is Mixture of Experts (MoE), and how does it optimize compute usage?
lessons.content_html:
Definition

Mixture of Experts (MoE) is a model architecture where multiple smaller sub-models (experts) exist, but only a subset of them are activated per input, instead of using the entire model.

Why it is used

  • Scale model capacity without proportional compute cost

  • Improve efficiency by using only relevant parts of the model

  • Enable high performance with lower inference cost

  • Handle diverse tasks with specialized experts

How it works (step-by-step)

  1. Input is passed to a gating network (router)

  2. The router selects top-k relevant experts (e.g., 2 out of 100)

  3. Only selected experts process the input

  4. Outputs from selected experts are combined

  5. Final result is returned

Key components

  • Experts: Independent sub-networks (usually feedforward layers)

  • Gating network (router): Decides which experts to use

  • Top-k selection: Limits number of active experts

  • Load balancing: Ensures experts are evenly utilized

Why it optimizes compute

  • Traditional models: All parameters used for every request

  • MoE models: Only a fraction of parameters used per request

  • Result:

    • Same or larger model capacity

    • Much lower compute per inference

Advantages

  • Efficient scaling to very large models

  • Lower inference cost compared to dense models

  • Specialization improves performance

  • Flexible and scalable architecture

Disadvantages

  • More complex training and routing

  • Load balancing challenges (some experts overused)

  • Communication overhead in distributed systems

Real-world example

A large MoE model with 100 experts:

  • For each query, only 2 experts are used

  • Achieves performance of a large model

  • But compute cost is similar to a much smaller model

Short interview-ready answer

Mixture of Experts (MoE) is an architecture where multiple expert sub-models exist, but only a few are activated per input using a gating network. This allows the model to scale in size while keeping computation efficient, as only a subset of parameters is used for each request, reducing cost and improving performance.

lessons.lesson_title: What challenges arise when managing GPUs for LLM workloads?
lessons.content_html:
Definition

Managing GPUs for LLM workloads involves efficiently allocating and utilizing GPU resources to handle model inference and training at scale without bottlenecks or waste.

Why it is used

  • GPUs are expensive and limited resources

  • LLMs require high compute and memory

  • Efficient management improves performance and reduces cost

How it works (step-by-step)

  1. Deploy models on GPU-enabled infrastructure

  2. Assign incoming requests to available GPUs

  3. Optimize usage via batching and parallelism

  4. Monitor GPU utilization and memory

  5. Scale up/down based on demand

  6. Handle failures or overload conditions

Key components

  • GPU scheduler: Assigns workloads to GPUs

  • Batching system: Combines requests for efficiency

  • Memory manager: Handles VRAM usage

  • Monitoring tools: Track utilization, temperature, errors

  • Orchestration: Kubernetes, Ray, etc.

Common challenges

Resource underutilization

  • GPUs idle due to poor scheduling

  • Low throughput

Memory constraints

  • Large models exceed VRAM

  • Leads to out-of-memory (OOM) errors

Fragmentation

  • Inefficient memory allocation reduces usable space

Latency vs throughput trade-off

  • Batching improves throughput but increases latency

Scaling complexity

  • Difficult to scale GPUs dynamically

  • Provisioning delays

Multi-tenancy issues

  • Multiple workloads competing for same GPU

  • Performance interference

Data transfer overhead

  • CPU ↔ GPU transfer adds latency

Fault tolerance

  • GPU failures can disrupt workloads

Solutions / best practices

Efficient batching

  • Group requests to maximize GPU utilization

Model optimization

  • Quantization, pruning, smaller models

GPU sharing

  • Use techniques like MIG or time-slicing

Auto-scaling

  • Scale GPU instances based on load

Smart scheduling

  • Route workloads based on GPU availability and type

Memory optimization

  • Use optimized inference engines (vLLM, TensorRT)

Caching

  • Cache results to reduce repeated GPU usage

Monitoring

  • Track utilization, memory, and errors in real time

Advantages

  • Better GPU utilization

  • Lower infrastructure cost

  • Improved system performance

Disadvantages

  • High system complexity

  • Requires specialized infrastructure

  • Hard to balance latency and throughput

Real-world example

A production LLM service:

  • Uses batching to increase GPU utilization

  • Applies quantization to fit models in memory

  • Uses Kubernetes to auto-scale GPU pods

  • Result: handles high traffic efficiently

Short interview-ready answer

Managing GPUs for LLM workloads involves challenges like underutilization, memory limits, batching trade-offs, and scaling complexity. These are addressed using techniques like efficient batching, smart scheduling, GPU sharing, model optimization, and auto-scaling, ensuring high utilization, low latency, and cost efficiency.

lessons.lesson_title: How do distributed computing techniques improve LLM scalability?
lessons.content_html:
Definition

Distributed computing for LLMs means splitting computation across multiple machines/GPUs so large models and high traffic can be handled efficiently.

Why it is used

  • LLMs are too large for a single GPU

  • Handle high concurrent requests

  • Reduce latency and improve throughput

  • Enable training and serving at scale

How it works (step-by-step)

  1. Break model or workload into smaller parts

  2. Distribute parts across multiple GPUs/nodes

  3. Process tasks in parallel

  4. Communicate intermediate results between nodes

  5. Aggregate outputs and return final response

Key components

  • Cluster of machines/GPUs: Distributed infrastructure

  • Communication layer: Data exchange (NCCL, RPC)

  • Orchestration: Kubernetes, Ray, etc.

  • Parallelism strategy: Defines how work is split

  • Load balancer: Distributes requests

Common techniques

Data parallelism

  • Same model on multiple GPUs

  • Each handles different requests/batches

  • Improves throughput

Model parallelism

  • Split model across GPUs

  • Each GPU handles part of the model

  • Useful for very large models

Pipeline parallelism

  • Split model into stages

  • Each GPU processes a stage sequentially

  • Improves utilization

Tensor parallelism

  • Split individual layers across GPUs

  • Enables fine-grained parallelism

Distributed inference

  • Serve requests across multiple nodes

  • Scale horizontally

Advantages

  • Scales to very large models

  • Handles high traffic efficiently

  • Improves performance and throughput

  • Enables faster training and inference

Disadvantages

  • Complex setup and coordination

  • Communication overhead between nodes

  • Harder debugging and monitoring

Real-world example

A large LLM:

  • Model split across 4 GPUs (model parallelism)

  • Requests distributed across multiple nodes (data parallelism)

  • System handles thousands of users simultaneously

Short interview-ready answer

Distributed computing improves LLM scalability by splitting workloads across multiple GPUs or machines using techniques like data, model, and pipeline parallelism. This allows systems to handle larger models and higher traffic efficiently, improving throughput and reducing latency while enabling scalable training and inference.

lessons.lesson_title: What factors influence the choice between cloud and on-premise deployment?
lessons.content_html:
Definition

Choosing between cloud and on-premise deployment means deciding where your LLM system runs:

  • Cloud: Hosted by providers (AWS, GCP, Azure)

  • On-premise: Runs on your own infrastructure and hardware

Why it is used

  • Optimize cost and performance

  • Meet security and compliance requirements

  • Control scalability and infrastructure

  • Align with business needs

How it works (decision flow)

  1. Evaluate workload size and traffic patterns

  2. Check data sensitivity and compliance needs

  3. Estimate cost (short-term vs long-term)

  4. Assess scalability requirements

  5. Consider operational complexity

  6. Choose cloud, on-prem, or hybrid setup

Key factors

Cost

  • Cloud: Pay-as-you-go, good for variable workloads

  • On-prem: High upfront cost, cheaper long-term at scale

Scalability

  • Cloud: Easy auto-scaling

  • On-prem: Limited by hardware capacity

Performance

  • Cloud: Depends on region/network latency

  • On-prem: Low latency if close to users/data

Security & compliance

  • Cloud: Managed security but shared environment

  • On-prem: Full control over sensitive data

Maintenance

  • Cloud: Managed by provider

  • On-prem: Requires in-house expertise

Flexibility

  • Cloud: Quick setup, easy experimentation

  • On-prem: More control but slower to adapt

Advantages

Cloud

  • Fast deployment

  • Auto-scaling

  • No hardware management

On-premise

  • Full data control

  • Predictable cost at scale

  • Custom hardware optimization

Disadvantages

Cloud

  • Ongoing operational cost

  • Vendor dependency

  • Data privacy concerns

On-premise

  • High upfront investment

  • Maintenance overhead

  • Limited scalability

Real-world example

A startup building an AI chatbot:

  • Uses cloud for quick scaling and low upfront cost
    A large enterprise with sensitive data:

  • Uses on-prem for security and compliance

Short interview-ready answer

The choice between cloud and on-premise depends on factors like cost, scalability, security, and maintenance. Cloud offers flexibility, auto-scaling, and low upfront cost, while on-premise provides greater control, security, and predictable long-term cost. Many systems use a hybrid approach to balance these trade-offs.

lessons.lesson_title: How do vector databases differ from traditional databases in LLM systems?
lessons.content_html:
Definition

Vector databases store and search data as embeddings (numerical vectors) based on semantic meaning, while traditional databases store structured data (rows/columns) and retrieve it using exact matches or filters.

Why it is used

  • Enable semantic search (meaning-based, not keyword-based)

  • Power Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

  • Handle unstructured data like text, images, embeddings

How it works (step-by-step)

Vector database

  1. Convert text/data into embeddings (vectors)

  2. Store vectors in the database

  3. Convert user query into a vector

  4. Perform similarity search (e.g., cosine similarity)

  5. Return most relevant results

Traditional database

  1. Store structured data (tables, rows)

  2. Query using SQL (filters, joins, exact match)

  3. Return matching records

Key components

Vector database

  • Embeddings: Vector representation of data

  • Similarity search: Nearest neighbor search (ANN)

  • Indexing: Optimized for fast vector search (HNSW, FAISS)

Traditional database

  • Schema: Tables, columns, relationships

  • Query engine: SQL-based queries

  • Indexes: B-trees, hash indexes

Key differences

Search type

  • Vector DB: Semantic (meaning-based)

  • Traditional DB: Exact match / rule-based

Data type

  • Vector DB: Unstructured (text, images, embeddings)

  • Traditional DB: Structured (rows, columns)

Query method

  • Vector DB: Similarity search (distance metrics)

  • Traditional DB: SQL queries

Use case

  • Vector DB: RAG, recommendation, semantic search

  • Traditional DB: Transactions, analytics, structured queries

Advantages

Vector database

  • Finds relevant results even without exact keywords

  • Handles unstructured data

  • Improves LLM response quality

Traditional database

  • Strong consistency and transactions

  • Efficient for structured data

  • Mature ecosystem

Disadvantages

Vector database

  • Less suitable for exact queries

  • Approximate results (ANN)

  • Additional complexity

Traditional database

  • Cannot understand semantic meaning

  • Poor performance for similarity search

Real-world example

A chatbot using RAG:

  • Vector DB retrieves relevant document chunks based on meaning

  • Traditional DB stores user profiles and metadata

Short interview-ready answer

Vector databases store and retrieve data using embeddings and similarity search, enabling semantic understanding, while traditional databases use structured schemas and exact queries. In LLM systems, vector databases are used for tasks like semantic search and RAG, whereas traditional databases handle structured data and transactions.
